## Where this landed

Starting from "OAuth flows are failing more often than not," the session produced:

**[PR #506](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/506)** — twelve commits. Five reference-parity fixes, each traced to a specific production symptom; two migrations; and a conformance suite that grew from nothing to 26 tests across five files.

**[MM-502](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-502/oauth-conformance-cover-the-wallet-device-key-consent-path)** — the wallet consent path, filed with the two pieces of infrastructure it needs and why it matters most (the password path structurally cannot carry the DPoP binding this PR added).

## What I'd want a reviewer to look at hardest

Three judgment calls where I chose not to do the expedient thing:

- **The SDK oracle isn't landed.** Making it run hermetically required relaxing our RFC 8414 https-issuer rule to satisfy a test. I stopped and documented the blocker instead. Its one run still paid for itself by finding that we never implemented loopback client identifiers.
- **No DPoP binding on the password consent path.** A hidden form field is attacker-controllable; a binding an attacker can omit is worse than none because it reads as protection. The code says so explicitly.
- **Two refresh behaviors stay in Rust tests** — stale-reuse revocation needs a 60-second wait, and the absolute session lifetime simply isn't observable from outside. Both are in the README's gap list rather than quietly absent.

The claim I'd treat most carefully is that these fixes resolve *your* reported failures. rpg.actor and the 23:14Z 401 burst fit the error-shape diagnosis cleanly. pckt.blog I traced to its callback leg without being able to attribute it definitively from server logs, and Beacon never reached the PDS at all. Re-running those two logins after this hits staging is what would actually close them.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

I'm seeing a critical security issue flagged by CodeRabbit around the loopback client metadata — specifically that an open redirect vulnerability could be synthesized where a malicious redirect URI like `http://localhost?redirect_uri=https://attacker.example/cb` might be accepted. I need to carefully verify whether this is a real vulnerability in my implementation, since the loopback spec should strictly enforce that redirect URIs are actually loopback addresses.

Looking at the attack chain: an attacker could craft a client_id with an embedded redirect parameter, and if my synthesis doesn't validate the redirect_uri against the loopback schema, it would pass through to the PAR validation. The `validate_private_use_redirect` function would exempt it early since the client_id scheme is http. However, I'm realizing this might not be a practical attack since the attacker controls both the client_id and redirect — they'd need to trick a user into approving consent for what appears to be a loopback client, which is the real phishing risk here.

But this is definitely a spec violation regardless of exploitability. The loopback exemption is supposed to restrict redirects to loopback addresses only, and my implementation isn't enforcing that. I need to fix this and then review all the other findings systematically before triaging them as a batch.

3	//! The ATProto OAuth client resolver: `client_id` URL policy + client-metadata-document fetch.
4	//!
5	//! Gathers: a URL-shaped OAuth `client_id` + the shared outbound HTTP client.
6	//! Processes: URL policy validation (pure) → metadata-document fetch (shell) →
7	//! document validation (pure).
8	//! Returns: the raw client-metadata JSON for the caller to cache, or a typed refusal.
9	//!
10	//! ATProto OAuth clients identify themselves by the URL of their client-metadata
11	//! document; authorization servers resolve unknown client_ids by fetching that URL
12	//! (<https://atproto.com/specs/oauth>). The fetched URL is caller-controlled, so the
13	//! policy check runs before any network I/O: https is required everywhere except
14	//! loopback hosts, which may use plain http (the spec's local-development exception —
15	//! also what lets tests serve metadata from 127.0.0.1). Failed resolutions land in a
16	//! process-local 60s negative cache (bounded, oldest-evicted) so replaying one failing
17	//! client_id against the unauthenticated PAR/authorize endpoints can't loop outbound
18	//! fetches.
19	//!
20	//! Also owns `validate_private_use_redirect`, the reverse-FQDN redirect rule both
21	//! request surfaces enforce. Consumers: `routes/oauth_par.rs` and
22	//! `routes/oauth_authorize.rs` (`resolve_client_metadata`), and
23	//! `routes/oauth_client_metadata.rs` (`url_is_loopback`).
24	
25	use std::collections::HashMap;
26	use std::sync::{Mutex, OnceLock};
27	use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
28	
29	use url::{Host, Url};
30	
31	/// Upper bound on an accepted client-metadata document. Real documents are well under
32	/// 4 KiB; the cap only exists so a hostile URL can't stream an unbounded body into memory.
33	const MAX_METADATA_BYTES: usize = 64 * 1024;
34	
35	/// Fetch timeout for the metadata document, independent of (and tighter than) the shared
36	/// client's default: PAR is interactive and a slow metadata host shouldn't hold it long.
37	const FETCH_TIMEOUT: std::time::Duration = std::time::Duration::from_secs(5);
38	
39	/// How long a failed resolution is remembered before the same client_id may trigger
40	/// another outbound fetch. Long enough to blunt replaying one failing URL against the
41	/// unauthenticated PAR/authorize endpoints; short enough that a client developer fixing
42	/// their metadata document isn't locked out meaningfully.
43	const NEGATIVE_CACHE_TTL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60);
44	
45	/// Bound on remembered failures so an attacker rotating client_ids can't grow the map
46	/// without limit; on overflow the oldest entry is evicted (the one closest to expiry).
47	const NEGATIVE_CACHE_MAX: usize = 1024;
48	
49	/// Recently failed resolutions, keyed by client_id. Process-local by design: this is a
50	/// throttle on *our own outbound fetches*, not a correctness cache, so losing it on
51	/// restart costs nothing. Successful resolutions are cached durably by the callers
52	/// (`oauth_clients` rows); only failures need remembering here.
53	fn negative_cache() -> &'static Mutex<HashMap<String, Instant>> {
54	    static CACHE: OnceLock<Mutex<HashMap<String, Instant>>> = OnceLock::new();
55	    CACHE.get_or_init(|| Mutex::new(HashMap::new()))
56	}
57	
58	/// Whether this client_id failed to resolve within the negative-cache TTL.
59	fn recently_failed(client_id: &str) -> bool {
60	    let cache = negative_cache().lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
61	    cache
62	        .get(client_id)
63	        .is_some_and(|at| at.elapsed() < NEGATIVE_CACHE_TTL)
64	}
65	
66	/// Record a failed resolution, expiring stale entries and evicting the oldest on overflow.
67	fn record_failure(client_id: &str) {
68	    let mut cache = negative_cache().lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
69	    cache.retain(|_, at| at.elapsed() < NEGATIVE_CACHE_TTL);
70	    if cache.len() >= NEGATIVE_CACHE_MAX {
71	        if let Some(oldest) = cache
72	            .iter()
73	            .min_by_key(|(_, at)| **at)
74	            .map(|(k, _)| k.clone())
75	        {
76	            cache.remove(&oldest);
77	        }
78	    }
79	    cache.insert(client_id.to_string(), Instant::now());
80	}
81	
82	/// Why a URL client_id could not be resolved to a usable client-metadata document.
83	///
84	/// The `Display` text becomes the OAuth `error_description`, so each message names the
85	/// problem from the client developer's point of view.
86	#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
87	pub enum ClientResolutionError {
88	    #[error("client_id is not a valid URL")]
89	    InvalidUrl,
90	
91	    #[error("client_id must be an https URL (plain http is allowed for loopback hosts only)")]
92	    InsecureUrl,
93	
94	    #[error("client_id URL must not contain credentials or a fragment")]
95	    ForbiddenUrlParts,
96	
97	    #[error("failed to fetch client metadata: {0}")]
98	    Fetch(String),
99	
100	    #[error("client metadata document exceeds {MAX_METADATA_BYTES} bytes")]
101	    TooLarge,
102	
103	    #[error("client metadata document is not valid JSON")]
104	    InvalidJson,
105	
106	    #[error(
107	        "client metadata client_id mismatch (the document must declare the URL it is served from)"
108	    )]
109	    ClientIdMismatch,
110	
111	    #[error("client metadata resolution for this client_id recently failed; retry shortly")]
112	    RecentlyFailed,
113	
114	    /// A loopback client_id encodes its own metadata, so a malformed one is rejected here
115	    /// rather than at a fetch that never happens.
116	    #[error("invalid loopback client_id: {0}")]
117	    InvalidDocument(&'static str),
118	}
119	
120	/// Validate the URL policy for a metadata-URL client_id (pure; no I/O).
121	///
122	/// Rules: parseable; https (http only for loopback hosts); no userinfo; no fragment.
123	fn validate_client_id_url(client_id: &str) -> Result<Url, ClientResolutionError> {
124	    let url = Url::parse(client_id).map_err(|_| ClientResolutionError::InvalidUrl)?;
125	
126	    match url.scheme() {
127	        "https" => {}
128	        "http" if host_is_loopback(&url) => {}
129	        _ => return Err(ClientResolutionError::InsecureUrl),
130	    }
131	
132	    if !url.username().is_empty() || url.password().is_some() || url.fragment().is_some() {
133	        return Err(ClientResolutionError::ForbiddenUrlParts);
134	    }
135	
136	    Ok(url)
137	}
138	
139	fn host_is_loopback(url: &Url) -> bool {
140	    match url.host() {
141	        Some(Host::Domain(d)) => d.eq_ignore_ascii_case("localhost"),
142	        Some(Host::Ipv4(ip)) => ip.is_loopback(),
143	        Some(Host::Ipv6(ip)) => ip.is_loopback(),
144	        None => false,
145	    }
146	}
147	
148	/// Whether a URL string's host is loopback (pure; unparseable → false). Shared policy
149	/// point: loopback is the one place plain-http client_ids and locally-derived (rather
150	/// than canonical) wallet client_ids are acceptable.
151	pub(crate) fn url_is_loopback(url: &str) -> bool {
152	    Url::parse(url)
153	        .map(|u| host_is_loopback(&u))
154	        .unwrap_or(false)
155	}
156	
157	/// Validate a fetched metadata document against the client_id it was fetched from (pure).
158	///
159	/// Per the ATProto OAuth spec the document MUST declare its own URL as `client_id` —
160	/// this is what stops one origin from impersonating another origin's client.
161	fn validate_metadata_document(client_id: &str, body: &str) -> Result<(), ClientResolutionError> {
162	    let doc: serde_json::Value =
163	        serde_json::from_str(body).map_err(|_| ClientResolutionError::InvalidJson)?;
164	
165	    if doc.get("client_id").and_then(|v| v.as_str()) != Some(client_id) {
166	        return Err(ClientResolutionError::ClientIdMismatch);
167	    }
168	
169	    Ok(())
170	}

3	//! Storage adapter for OAuth server-side state: the client registry
4	//! (register/upsert/get), authorization codes, the persistent ES256 signing key,
5	//! DPoP-bound refresh tokens, and PAR requests — plus the expiry-cleanup sweeps for
6	//! codes, tokens, and PAR rows.

8	use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
9	use sqlx::SqlitePool;
10	
11	/// A registered OAuth client row from the `oauth_clients` table.
12	///
13	/// `client_metadata` is stored as a raw JSON string (RFC 7591 client metadata).
14	/// Callers are responsible for serializing/deserializing the JSON.
15	pub struct OAuthClientRow {
16	    // client_id is redundant with the lookup key at every handler call site (kept so a
17	    // row is self-describing; read by tests), same posture as created_at below.
18	    #[allow(dead_code)]
19	    pub client_id: String,
20	    pub client_metadata: String,
21	    // created_at is unread by handlers (kept for audit value: admin listing, DCR).
22	    #[allow(dead_code)]
23	    pub created_at: String,
24	}
25	
26	/// Subset of RFC 7591 client metadata fields used by the authorization and PAR endpoints.
27	///
28	/// Deserialized from `OAuthClientRow::client_metadata` (a raw JSON string) by the
29	/// authorization and PAR handlers.
30	#[derive(Deserialize, Default)]
31	pub struct ClientMetadata {
32	    #[serde(default)]
33	    pub redirect_uris: Vec<String>,
34	    pub client_name: Option<String>,
35	    /// `none` (public) or `private_key_jwt` (confidential). Absent = `none`.
36	    pub token_endpoint_auth_method: Option<String>,
37	    /// Inline JWK set for `private_key_jwt` assertion verification. Kept as raw JSON here;
38	    /// the token endpoint's client-auth module parses it.
39	    pub jwks: Option<serde_json::Value>,
40	    /// JWK-set URL alternative to `jwks` (client-controlled — the consumer policy-checks
41	    /// and fetches it with the SSRF-hardened client).
42	    pub jwks_uri: Option<String>,
43	}
44	
45	/// Register a new OAuth client.
46	///
47	/// `client_id` is an HTTPS URL (the client's metadata document URL per AT Protocol OAuth spec).
48	/// `client_metadata` is a JSON string conforming to RFC 7591 client metadata.
49	///
50	/// Returns `sqlx::Error` on failure. Callers should use `crate::db::is_unique_violation`
51	/// to detect duplicate `client_id` conflicts.
52	///
53	/// Unwired: no handler registers clients dynamically (RFC 7591).
54	#[allow(dead_code)]
55	pub async fn register_oauth_client(
56	    pool: &SqlitePool,
57	    client_id: &str,
58	    client_metadata: &str,
59	) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> {
60	    sqlx::query(
61	        "INSERT INTO oauth_clients (client_id, client_metadata, created_at) \
62	         VALUES (?, ?, datetime('now'))",
63	    )
64	    .bind(client_id)
65	    .bind(client_metadata)
66	    .execute(pool)
67	    .await?;
68	    Ok(())
69	}
70	
71	/// Insert or refresh a resolved OAuth client's metadata (the URL-client_id cache).
72	///
73	/// Unlike [`register_oauth_client`], a conflict on `client_id` replaces the stored
74	/// metadata instead of failing: the row is a cache of a document the client controls,
75	/// and two concurrent PARs resolving the same client must not race into a 500.
76	pub async fn upsert_oauth_client(
77	    pool: &SqlitePool,
78	    client_id: &str,
79	    client_metadata: &str,
80	) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> {
81	    sqlx::query(
82	        "INSERT INTO oauth_clients (client_id, client_metadata, created_at) \
83	         VALUES (?, ?, datetime('now')) \
84	         ON CONFLICT(client_id) DO UPDATE SET client_metadata = excluded.client_metadata",
85	    )
86	    .bind(client_id)
87	    .bind(client_metadata)
88	    .execute(pool)
89	    .await?;
90	    Ok(())
91	}
92	
93	/// Look up a registered OAuth client by `client_id`. Returns `None` if not found.
94	pub async fn get_oauth_client(
95	    pool: &SqlitePool,
96	    client_id: &str,
97	) -> Result<Option<OAuthClientRow>, sqlx::Error> {
98	    let row: Option<(String, String, String)> = sqlx::query_as(
99	        "SELECT client_id, client_metadata, created_at FROM oauth_clients WHERE client_id = ?",
100	    )
101	    .bind(client_id)
102	    .fetch_optional(pool)
103	    .await?;
104	
105	    Ok(
106	        row.map(|(client_id, client_metadata, created_at)| OAuthClientRow {
107	            client_id,
108	            client_metadata,
109	            created_at,
110	        }),
111	    )
112	}

attachment.snippet:
1	# OAuth interop audit — why third-party atproto apps fail against Custos
2	
3	Date: 2026-08-03. Prompted by mixed real-world results: tangled works, rpg.actor logs in but
4	actions fail, pckt.blog dies mid-flow, Beacon (beaconbits.app) can't log in at all. This audit
5	diffs our OAuth surface against the reference `@atproto/oauth-provider` (what bsky.social runs,
6	August 2026 state) and tranquil-pds, and correlates the gaps with production log evidence.
7	
8	## Live evidence (Railway, pds.obsign.org, 2026-08-01 → 08-03)
9	
10	- **rpg.actor** (20:57Z 08-03): full healthy login — PAR 201 → authorize → wallet approve →
11	  complete 303 → token 400 `use_dpop_nonce` → token 200. The nonce dance works. Whatever fails,
12	  fails *after* login.
13	- **pckt.blog** (20:56Z 08-03): skipped PAR entirely (direct `GET /oauth/authorize`, which we
14	  accept despite advertising `require_pushed_authorization_requests: true`), consent approved,
15	  `complete` 303'd back with the code — and **no token exchange ever arrived**. Five seconds
16	  later a bare `GET /oauth/authorize` returned 400. The flow dies on the client's callback leg.
17	- **Unattributed burst** (23:14Z 08-02): a bsky-deck-style client got uniform 401s on
18	  `getSession`, `getTimeline`, `getPreferences`, `chat.bsky.convo.getLog`, etc. — the signature
19	  of a session whose access token expired and whose client never managed to refresh.
20	- **Beacon**: zero trace in the current deployment's logs. Its failure either predates the log
21	  window or happens client-side before our PDS is ever contacted (client-metadata fetch,
22	  handle→PDS resolution, or metadata validation on their end).
23	- Recurring token-endpoint 400s are all `use_dpop_nonce`; most are followed by a successful
24	  retry (normal bootstrap), but several are not — consistent with clients that don't retry the
25	  nonce dance on *refresh* (see gap 4).
26	
27	## Client stacks involved
28	
29	| App | Stack | Scope style | Client auth |
30	|---|---|---|---|
31	| tangled.org | Rust `atproto-oauth` | granular `repo:sh.tangled.* rpc:sh.tangled.* blob:*/* identity:handle` | `private_key_jwt` (ES256) |
32	| rpg.actor | custom TS (PKCE+DPoP) | granular, repo-only: nine `repo:<nsid>` + `blob:image/*`, **no `rpc:`** | `none` |
33	| pckt.blog | custom (non-PAR!) | granular incl. `include:<nsid>` permission sets and `rpc:...?aud=did:web:marque.at#marque_registrar` | `none` |
34	| Beacon | unknown (metadata not fetchable at common paths) | unknown | unknown |
35	
36	The generational divide: everything that fails uses the 2026 granular scope grammar and/or a
37	non-official client stack; the transitional-scope, official-stack path is the one we validated
38	against (wallet, tangled after the `sub` fix).
39	
40	## Gap matrix vs the reference provider
41	
42	### P0 — actively breaking real apps
43	
44	1. **Gap 1.** Resource-call error shape is not atproto XRPC shape.** `common::ApiError` emits   `{"error": {"code": "TOKEN_EXPIRED", "message": ...}}` (nested, SCREAMING_SNAKE); atproto
45	   clients key refresh-on-401 off the flat `{"error": "ExpiredToken", "message": ...}` body
46	   (`@atproto/api`, indigo, atcute all match on the string `ExpiredToken`). The correctly named
47	   `ErrorCode::ExpiredToken` variant exists but is only used for password-reset tokens;
48	   `jwt.rs` returns `TokenExpired` for expired access tokens. Combined with our **300 s access
49	   tokens** (reference: 15 min, spec allows up to 30), every client session hits an
50	   unrecognizable expiry error within five minutes of login and never refreshes. This is the
51	   best single explanation for "logs in fine, actions around the site fail" (rpg.actor, and the
52	   23:14Z burst). Also: **no `WWW-Authenticate` header on any 401** anywhere in the tree, so
53	   spec-following clients can't even discover the failure class.
54	
55	2. **Gap 2.** `private_key_jwt` advertised but not implemented.** `TokenRequestForm` has no   `client_assertion`/`client_assertion_type` fields; serde silently drops them and the client
56	   is treated as public. Confidential clients (tangled!) currently "work" only because we skip
57	   their authentication entirely — an interop time bomb and a real security gap (a leaked
58	   authorization code for a confidential client is exchangeable by anyone holding the DPoP
59	   key). Either implement RFC 7523 client assertions (with clock tolerance — see reference
60	   issue #4474: allow ~30 s skew on `iat`) or stop advertising the method.
61	
62	3. **Gap 3.** `rpc:` scope `aud` matching is inconsistent with itself and the ecosystem.**   `xrpc_dispatch` passes the **raw `atproto-proxy` header including the `#serviceId`
63	   fragment** into `require_rpc`, while `getServiceAuth` strips the fragment before the same
64	   check; `aud_matches` is exact string equality. Meanwhile real clients are split on
65	   convention — pckt.blog's scopes carry `aud=did:web:marque.at#marque_registrar` (with
66	   fragment), the spec's examples use the bare DID. Result: a granular `rpc:` grant can pass
67	   one path and fail the other, and which one works depends on how the client wrote its scope
68	   string. Matching must normalize (compare DID, and treat fragment as an optional refinement)
69	   on both paths.
70	
71	4. **Gap 4.** Refresh semantics are far tighter than the ecosystem assumes.**   - Refresh-token TTL **24 h** (reference: 2 weeks public / 3 months confidential since
72	     June 2025, PR #3883). Any client idle a day is silently logged out.
73	   - Rotation is strictly single-use with **no reuse-detection grace window**: a concurrent
74	     double-refresh (multi-tab, mobile background+foreground) races; the loser's token is
75	     already deleted and the session strands. The reference keeps a short grace period and
76	     revokes the family on true reuse.
77	   - Every refresh **requires a fresh server nonce**, so refresh is always a
78	     `use_dpop_nonce` → retry two-step; clients that only implement the nonce dance at the
79	     initial exchange (common in hand-rolled stacks) fail here. The unretried
80	     `use_dpop_nonce` 400s in the logs fit this.
81	
82	### P1 — spec divergences that will bite specific clients
83	
84	1. **Gap 5.** PAR is advertised as required but not enforced** — direct `GET /oauth/authorize` works   (deliberate, documented). Harmless for lenient clients, but it means we never bind
85	   `dpop_jkt` at PAR time, and:
86	1. **Gap 6.** Authorization codes are not DPoP-key-bound at issuance** (no `jkt` column on the code   row) — the reference binds the key at PAR. Whoever presents the code binds it.
87	1. **Gap 7.** `state` is mandatory at PAR** — nonstandard (RECOMMENDED in OAuth; the atproto profile   does not require it). A client relying on PKCE alone gets `invalid_request`.
88	1. **Gap 8.** Client metadata is barely validated**: only `client_id` and `redirect_uris` are read.   `grant_types`, `response_types`, `scope`, `application_type`, `dpop_bound_access_tokens`,

   sovereign accounts go through the device-key path, not this password form. That is also the
   only path that carries a pushed request's DPoP key through to the issued code: the password
   form's pushed request is consumed by the GET that renders it, so the code is issued unbound

with open(p, "w") as f: f.write(src)

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix: address review — restrict loopback redirects, bound the jwks fetch

The security finding was real and mine. `loopback_client_metadata`
copied every `redirect_uri` query value into the synthesized document
unchecked, so `http://localhost?redirect_uri=https://attacker.example/cb`
produced a client whose authorization code left the machine: PAR's
`redirect_uris.contains()` passes because the attacker put the value
there, and the reverse-FQDN rule cannot catch it because that check
exempts non-https client_ids. Redirect targets are now restricted to
plain http on a loopback IP literal — `localhost` included in the
refusal, per RFC 8252 §8.3, since the name can be repointed to a
non-loopback interface.

The jwks_uri fetch gains a 64 KiB cap, matching the client-metadata
fetch beside it. The timeout half of that finding was already covered
by the shared hardened client.

Writing the end-to-end PAR key-binding test the review asked for
produced a more useful result than the test: it failed, because the
password consent path deliberately issues codes unbound (its pushed
request is consumed by the GET that renders the form, leaving only an
attacker-controllable hidden field to carry the key). So `dpop_jkt`
enforcement is reachable end-to-end only through the wallet consent
path, which has no coverage yet. The test now pins that gap instead of
asserting a guarantee that does not hold, and the changelog and README
no longer claim an intercepted code is unredeemable in general.

Also: flat-shape hygiene across the suite — the Bearer test now proves
the token works as DPoP first, so a 401 cannot pass for the wrong
reason; the runner fails when it discovers no test files; PAR and
consent statuses are asserted before their bodies are read; test
servers close keep-alive connections; locals no longer shadow the
node:test hooks. Plus doc accuracy: MD029-safe list prefixes that keep
the "gap N" references resolvable, a corrected audit status, and a
design plan that no longer points at an appendix that was never written.

Declined: flattening router-generated 405s (no atproto client
dispatches on 405; XRPC defines only GET and POST, and handler errors
already flatten) and tying a Rust test's aging offset to a SQL-modifier
string constant. Caching the jwks_uri fetch is legitimate but wants the
config-driven TTL/cooldown agent-auth already has — filed separately.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git push 2>&1 | tail -2

input.title: Cache the OAuth client jwks_uri fetch
input.description:
`resolve_client_key` in `crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_token/client_auth.rs` fetches a confidential client's `jwks_uri` on **every** token request that uses it. Two consequences:

- A client refreshing on the 15-minute access-token TTL adds an outbound round trip to its own key host on every refresh.
- An outage or slowdown at that host makes the client unable to authenticate at all, since there is no cached key to fall back on. The shared hardened client bounds how long it can hang, but the request still fails.

The repository already models the fix for agent-auth trusted issuers: `auth/jwks.rs`'s `JwksCache` with `jwks_cache_ttl_secs` and `jwks_refetch_cooldown_secs` in `crates/common/src/config.rs`. That cache also carries a per-URL refetch cooldown, which matters here for the same reason it does there — an unauthenticated caller naming arbitrary `kid`s should not be able to drive outbound fetches.

Reusing `JwksCache` looks like the right move rather than adding a second caching layer; it is already in `AppState` as `jwks_cache`. The main design question is whether confidential-client keys should share that cache instance with agent-auth issuers or get their own, since the two have different trust models and possibly different TTLs.

Raised by CodeRabbit on #506 and deliberately deferred there: the fetch was newly added in that PR and correct, just uncached, and wiring the config-driven cache is its own change.

Note the fetch is now size-capped (64 KiB) and the transport policy matches `client_id` resolution — that part is done.

content.text:
{"id":"MM-502","title":"OAuth conformance: cover the wallet (device-key) consent path","description":"The OAuth conformance suite added in #506 (`tools/oauth-conformance/`) drives every flow through the **password** consent form. Production logs show that real third-party logins to sovereign accounts go through the **wallet** path instead — the device-key-signed approve/complete endpoints in `crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_consent.rs`. So the consent leg that users actually exercise is the one leg the suite does not cover.

The protocol legs on either side of consent (PAR, token exchange, refresh, resource errors) are shared and are covered, so this is a real but bounded gap: what is untested is the approval ceremony itself and everything that depends on it.

## Why it matters

The consent paths are not equivalent. The password path could not carry the PAR-time DPoP key binding at all — its PAR row is consumed by the GET that renders the form, so the only carrier left is an attacker-controllable hidden field (see the comment in `oauth_authorize.rs`). The wallet path keeps its pending request server-side and **does** bind.

**Confirmed empirically during review of #506.** A conformance test written to prove the binding end-to-end failed: PAR accepted the DPoP proof, but a *different* key then redeemed the resulting code with a 200. So `dpop_jkt` enforcement is currently exercised end-to-end **nowhere** — the only coverage is a Rust unit test that writes the binding directly onto the code row, skipping the PAR and consent legs entirely. The failing test was kept, inverted to pin the gap (`flow.test.ts`, "a PAR DPoP proof is accepted, but the password consent path drops the binding"); it will fail and demand attention if the behaviour ever changes.

That raises this from a coverage gap to the thing standing between a shipped security control and any evidence it works.

## What it needs

Two pieces of infrastructure, neither of which exists today:

1. **A JS port of the OAuth consent envelope.** The canonical encoding lives only in Rust (`crates/crypto/src/oauth_consent.rs`): length-prefixed `name:len:value\n` in fixed field order, with `scopeHash` as lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the space-joined granted scope. There is a golden vector at `test-vectors/oauth-consent-envelope-v1.json` already consumed by a Rust test, so the port can be pinned against the identical file — the same pattern as the sovereign-session and account-delete envelopes.
2. **A mock [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) serving audit logs.** Wallet approval verifies the signature against the account's authoritative signing authority, resolved live from `/{did}/log/audit` (`identity/authority.rs` → `identity/plc.rs`). The suite's mock directory (`tools/oauth-conformance/test/mock-plc.ts`) currently serves DID documents only; it would need to serve a real audit-log array. The genesis op is available client-side from `tools/interop`'s `buildGenesisOp`, so the material exists.

Signing reuses `@atproto/crypto` via `tools/interop/src/crypto.js`, and the rotation key is already persisted in interop state as `rotationKeyPrivateHex`.

## Scope

* Port the consent envelope to TS, pinned against the existing golden vector.
* Extend the suite's mock plc to serve `/{did}/log/audit`.
* A `wallet-consent.test.ts` covering: preview by `user_code`, the device-key-signed approval, the number-match requirement when a push was dispatched (V060), completion issuing a code, and — the one the password path cannot reach — that a code issued through this path is bound to the PAR-time DPoP key and refuses a different one.

{"id":"MM-502","title":"OAuth conformance: cover the wallet (device-key) consent path","description":"The OAuth conformance suite added in #506 (`tools/oauth-conformance/`) drives every flow through the **password** consent form. Production logs show that real third-party logins to sovereign accounts go through the **wallet** path instead — the device-key-signed approve/complete endpoints in `crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_consent.rs`. So the consent leg that users actually exercise is the one leg the suite does not cover.

The protocol legs on either side of consent (PAR, token exchange, refresh, resource errors) are shared and are covered, so this is a real but bounded gap: what is untested is the approval ceremony itself and everything that depends on it.

## Why it matters

The consent paths are not equivalent. The password path could not carry the PAR-time DPoP key binding at all — its PAR row is consumed by the GET that renders the form, so the only carrier left is an attacker-controllable hidden field (see the comment in `oauth_authorize.rs`). The wallet path keeps its pending request server-side and **does** bind.

**Confirmed empirically during review of #506.** A conformance test written to prove the binding end-to-end failed: PAR accepted the DPoP proof, but a *different* key then redeemed the resulting code with a 200. So `dpop_jkt` enforcement is currently exercised end-to-end **nowhere** — the only coverage is a Rust unit test that writes the binding directly onto the code row, skipping the PAR and consent legs entirely. The failing test was kept, inverted to pin the gap (`flow.test.ts`, "a PAR DPoP proof is accepted, but the password consent path drops the binding"); it will fail and demand attention if the behaviour ever changes.

That raises this from a coverage gap to the thing standing between a shipped security control and any evidence it works.

## What it needs

Two pieces of infrastructure, neither of which exists today:

1. **A JS port of the OAuth consent envelope.** The canonical encoding lives only in Rust (`crates/crypto/src/oauth_consent.rs`): length-prefixed `name:len:value\n` in fixed field order, with `scopeHash` as lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the space-joined granted scope. There is a golden vector at `test-vectors/oauth-consent-envelope-v1.json` already consumed by a Rust test, so the port can be pinned against the identical file — the same pattern as the sovereign-session and account-delete envelopes.
2. **A mock [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) serving audit logs.** Wallet approval verifies the signature against the account's authoritative signing authority, resolved live from `/{did}/log/audit` (`identity/authority.rs` → `identity/plc.rs`). The suite's mock directory (`tools/oauth-conformance/test/mock-plc.ts`) currently serves DID documents only; it would need to serve a real audit-log array. The genesis op is available client-side from `tools/interop`'s `buildGenesisOp`, so the material exists.

Signing reuses `@atproto/crypto` via `tools/interop/src/crypto.js`, and the rotation key is already persisted in interop state as `rotationKeyPrivateHex`.

## Scope

* Port the consent envelope to TS, pinned against the existing golden vector.
* Extend the suite's mock plc to serve `/{did}/log/audit`.
* A `wallet-consent.test.ts` covering: preview by `user_code`, the device-key-signed approval, the number-match requirement when a push was dispatched (V060), completion issuing a code, and — the one the password path cannot reach — that a code issued through this path is bound to the PAR-time DPoP key and refuses a different one.
* A replayed approval envelope must win nothing (the guarded single-use transition).

## Out of scope

Anything requiring a real device or push delivery; the envelope is signed in-process by the test.

**2026-08-03 OAuth gap audit vs the reference `@atproto/oauth-provider`.** Full writeup: `docs/2026-08-03-oauth-interop-audit.md`. Prompted by real failures: tangled worked, rpg.actor logged in but actions failed, pckt.blog died mid-flow, Beacon couldn't log in.

**Five fixes shipped same day** on branch `claude/oauth-atproto-failures-4ff55e` (unreleased at time of writing, 6 commits, all `just ci-pds`-equivalent checks green):

1. **Flat XRPC error shape** (`e0fcd2f2`) — we emitted the provisioning API's nested `{"error":{"code":"TOKEN_EXPIRED"}}` on `/xrpc/*`; atproto clients only refresh on flat `{"error":"ExpiredToken"}`. Fix = a boundary middleware (`crates/pds/src/xrpc_error_shape.rs`) that re-encodes `ApiError` responses on `/xrpc/*` only, using `ErrorCode::xrpc_name()`. `/v1/*` keeps the nested envelope. **Verified bsky.social's real wire names via curl** (`AuthMissing`, `InvalidToken`).
2. **Token lifetimes + refresh** (`28c9e25d`, **V061**) — access 300s→900s; refresh 24h→14 days *absolute* (rotation carries expiry forward, never extends); session families via `session_id` + `superseded_at`, with a 60s grace window so a concurrent duplicate refresh still rotates instead of stranding the loser, and stale reuse revoking the whole family.
3. **`rpc:` aud fragment normalization** (`0b04bdb4`) — proxy path passed the raw `atproto-proxy` header *with* `#fragment`, `getServiceAuth` stripped it; now both compare bare DIDs.
4. **`private_key_jwt`** (`3cfdaf3b`) — was advertised but `client_assertion` was silently dropped by serde. New `oauth_token/client_auth.rs`; 30s clock tolerance (atproto#4474 trap).
5. **DPoP binding at PAR + optional `state`** (`bfd3f8c8`, **V062**) — `dpop_jkt` carried PAR→code, enforced at token exchange. Deliberately NOT bound on the direct authorize path or the password-consent POST (its PAR row is consumed by the GET, so only an attacker-controllable hidden field remains) — the wallet path keeps server-side state and does bind.

**Still open:** (6) a multi-client conformance harness in CI — every gap here was invisible because we only ever tested our own clients; (7) instrumented repros of pckt.blog (dies on its callback leg before ever POSTing `/oauth/token` — needs client-side capture) and Beacon (never reaches the PDS at all). **Nothing is verified against a live third-party client yet.**

Sibling: [[project-oauth-token-sub-did]] (same lesson, earlier instance).

All 23 threads triaged, fixed or declined with reasons, and resolved. Pushed as `06839f9f`; CI is re-running and I'm watching it.

## CodeRabbit was right about something important

**The loopback `redirect_uri` finding was a real vulnerability in code I wrote.** I traced the full chain before accepting it: my synthesis copied every `redirect_uri` query value verbatim, PAR's `redirect_uris.contains()` then passes because the attacker put the value there, and the reverse-FQDN rule can't catch it because that check exempts non-https client_ids. So `http://localhost?redirect_uri=https://attacker.example/cb` produced a client whose authorization code left the machine. Now restricted to loopback IP literals, with `localhost` also refused per RFC 8252 §8.3 — the name can be repointed to a non-loopback interface. Five hostile shapes are covered by a test.

## And its test request found something worse

CodeRabbit asked for an end-to-end PAR key-binding test. Writing it produced a better result than the test would have: **it failed.** The password consent path deliberately issues codes *unbound* — its pushed request is consumed by the GET that renders the form, leaving only an attacker-controllable hidden field to carry the key. I'd documented that design decision in the code, but I had not connected it to the consequence:

**`dpop_jkt` enforcement is currently reachable end-to-end nowhere.** The only path that binds is the wallet path, which has no coverage; the enforcement itself is tested only by a Rust unit test that writes the binding straight onto the code row, skipping PAR and consent entirely.

So I'd overclaimed. The changelog and PR body said an intercepted code "cannot be redeemed by anyone else" — true only on the wallet path. Both are corrected, the failing test is kept and inverted to pin the gap (so it fails loudly if the behavior ever changes), and **MM-502 is raised to Urgent**: it's what stands between a shipped security control and any evidence it works.

## The rest

Also fixed: the `jwks_uri` size cap (the timeout half of that finding was already covered), the Bearer test that could pass for the wrong reason, a runner that would have passed silently on zero discovered tests, plus doc-accuracy items. Suite is at 27 tests, all green locally, with 2337 Rust tests and clippy clean.

**Declined three**, with reasons in the PR: flattening router-generated 405s (XRPC defines only GET/POST — no client dispatches on 405), tying a Rust test's aging offset to a SQL-modifier *string* constant, and moving protocol constraints out of call-site comments into an ADR. **Deferred one** as [MM-503](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-503/cache-the-oauth-client-jwks-uri-fetch): caching the `jwks_uri` fetch wants the config-driven TTL/cooldown `auth/jwks.rs` already has, which is its own change.

Worth noting the pattern: the two most valuable things this review surfaced both came from *attempting* something rather than reasoning about it — same as the SDK oracle finding loopback clients before it completed a flow.

content.thinking:
The `cargo audit` failure is coming from RustSec advisories in dependencies, not my code itself. I need to check the audit output to see which specific vulnerability triggered the failure—since warnings alone don't cause failures unless `deny = warnings` is set. Looking at the advisory database, it seems like `RUSTSEC-2026-0221` related to event-list might be the culprit, and this appears to be dependency drift from an updated advisory database rather than something I introduced.

Since `cargo audit` fetches the advisory database fresh on each run, a new advisory landing between runs would flip the gate. That's exactly what `.cargo/audit.toml` is for—managing ignored advisories with their rationale. I need to pull more of the log to see whether this is actually a vulnerability or a warning being denied by configuration.

content.subject: Fix 2: token lifetimes + refresh grace/reuse detection

content.subject: Fix 3: normalize rpc: scope aud matching across proxy and getServiceAuth
content.description: xrpc_dispatch passes raw atproto-proxy header (with #fragment) to require_rpc; getServiceAuth strips fragment. Normalize: match on DID, treat fragment as optional refinement, accept scopes written either way.

content.subject: Fix 4: implement private_key_jwt client auth + validate client metadata

content.subject: Fix 5: bind dpop_jkt at PAR/code issuance; make state optional

This advisory drift is unrelated to my PR and would block `main` too, but it's still blocking me. The right move is to add an ignore entry to `.cargo/audit.toml` with clear rationale — that's the established process for this. content.text: Two independent reasons it's unreachable: `rkyv` is an optional feature that isn't enabled, and `rust_decimal` itself only reaches the Tauri app shells — never the deployed Linux PDS. This is advisory-DB drift that would fail `main` equally. Adding the ignore with rationale, per the file's documented process:

input.command:
python3 - << 'PYEOF'
p = ".cargo/audit.toml"
with open(p) as f: src = f.read()
old = """ignore = [
    "RUSTSEC-2023-0071","""
new = """ignore = [
    "RUSTSEC-2023-0071",
    "RUSTSEC-2026-0235","""
assert old in src
src = src.replace(old, new, 1)

anchor = "\nignore = ["
rationale = """# RUSTSEC-2026-0235 — out-of-bounds reads validating `rkyv` archives containing Rc/Arc.
#   `rkyv` is never compiled: it is an *optional, disabled* feature of `rust_decimal`, so it
#   appears in Cargo.lock (which records the union of possible dependencies) but in no build
#   graph — `cargo tree -i rkyv --target all` reports "nothing to print" on every target.
#   Independently, `rust_decimal` itself reaches only the Tauri app shells
#   (`rust_decimal` ← `byte-unit` ← `tauri-plugin-log` ← identity-wallet / admin-companion),
#   never the deployed Linux PDS binary. The fix is a `rust_decimal` bump to a release
#   depending on `rkyv >=0.8.17`, which is outside this repo's control.
#
#   This is a lockfile-versus-feature-graph false positive: `cargo audit` scans the lockfile
#   and cannot see that the feature is off. Revisit if `rust_decimal` ever enables `rkyv` by
#   default, or when a bumped release lands.
"""
src = src.replace(anchor, "\n" + rationale + "\nignore = [", 1)
with open(p, "w") as f: f.write(src)
print("audit.toml updated")
PYEOF

content.description: Accept client_assertion (RFC 7523, ES256, 30s clock tolerance) at token/revoke endpoints; fetch client jwks/jwks_uri; enforce token_endpoint_auth_method from client metadata; validate grant_types/response_types/scope/dpop_bound_access_tokens.

content.subject: Fix 1: flat atproto error shape on /xrpc surface + wallet tolerant parser
content.description: Middleware flattens ApiError responses on /xrpc/* to {"error":"PascalName","message":...} with canonical XRPC names (ExpiredToken, InvalidToken, AuthMissing, AuthenticationRequired, RateLimitExceeded, InternalServerError...). Provisioning /v1/* keeps nested envelope. Wallet Rust parser becomes shape-tolerant. Update tests.

content.subject: Fix 2: token lifetimes + refresh grace/reuse detection
content.description: Access token 300s → 15 min; refresh TTL 24h → 2 weeks (rolling); add concurrent-refresh grace window (old refresh token remains exchangeable briefly for the same DPoP key / returns same result) and reuse detection.
content.activeForm: Extending token lifetimes and refresh semantics

content.subject: Fix 3: normalize rpc: scope aud matching across proxy and getServiceAuth
content.description: xrpc_dispatch passes raw atproto-proxy header (with #fragment) to require_rpc; getServiceAuth strips fragment. Normalize: match on DID, treat fragment as optional refinement, accept scopes written either way.

content.subject: Fix 4: implement private_key_jwt client auth + validate client metadata
content.description: Accept client_assertion (RFC 7523, ES256, 30s clock tolerance) at token/revoke endpoints; fetch client jwks/jwks_uri; enforce token_endpoint_auth_method from client metadata; validate grant_types/response_types/scope/dpop_bound_access_tokens.

content.subject: Fix 5: bind dpop_jkt at PAR/code issuance; make state optional
content.description: Store dpop_jkt from PAR DPoP proof (when present) on the pending authorization + auth code rows; enforce at token exchange. Drop the nonstandard mandatory state at PAR.

git add .cargo/audit.toml && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
chore: accept RUSTSEC-2026-0235 (rkyv), which is never compiled

Unrelated to this PR's changes — a fresh advisory landed in the RustSec
database between two runs on the same branch, so the audit gate went
red on the same Cargo.lock this PR never touches. main would fail
identically.

`rkyv` is not in any build graph. It is an *optional, disabled* feature
of `rust_decimal`, so it appears in Cargo.lock — which records the
union of possible dependencies — while `cargo tree -i rkyv --target all`
reports "nothing to print" on every target. Independently, rust_decimal
itself reaches only the Tauri app shells (rust_decimal ← byte-unit ←
tauri-plugin-log ← identity-wallet / admin-companion), never the
deployed Linux PDS binary. Either fact alone makes the advisory
unreachable here.

This is a lockfile-versus-feature-graph false positive: cargo audit
scans the lockfile and cannot see that the feature is off. The real fix
is a rust_decimal bump to a release depending on rkyv >=0.8.17, which
is outside this repo's control; the rationale records what to re-check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git push 2>&1 | tail -2
